en: Established in a concentrated mind during the Abhimukhī stage, he is oriented toward the qualities of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
One who has seen the reality of arising through dependence attains cessation by dwelling in wisdom;
just as a single person with eyes can go wherever he desires.
Just as an entire group of blind men is easily led to their destination by being guided,
so too does wisdom, taking hold of those who lack vision, lead them toward the virtues of Buddhahood. (6.2)
He understands those most profound phenomena both through scripture and through reasoning,
as well as according to the system of the noble Nāgārjuna.
I speak according to the actual state of things:
even while remaining an ordinary person, upon hearing of emptiness, one experiences joy within again and again.
He whose seed for the wisdom of a Perfectly Awakened One exists becomes one whose eyes are moistened and overflowing with faith, and whose body is covered in bristling hairs of joy. 6.4 (1)
And he is a fit vessel for the instruction in reality;
the ultimate truth should be told to him, for his qualities will follow from that. (6.5)
Always abiding by the undertaking of ethical discipline,
he practices generosity and cultivates compassion;
he endures all things, and that virtue is for the sake of awakening.
He indeed directs the world toward liberation.
Being discerning regarding the noble and profound method, he shows reverence toward the bodhisattvas.
People shall gradually attain the stage of Joy;
let those who seek that goal listen to this path.
How could those very things arise from them, much less from others?
Nor indeed from both, much less without a cause.
Therefore, there is no advantage whatsoever in its arising; and for that which has already been born, birth again is simply not logical. (6.8)
If birth were to be conceptually constructed for that which is already born, then sprouts and the like would never attain origination here;
and the seed itself would be subject to origination until the very end of existence.
For how indeed could its destruction come about through that very same thing?
(6.9) The differences in configuration, color, taste, potency, and maturation would not belong to your sprout as distinct from its cause.

If it were to abandon its prior nature and assume another form, how indeed could it possess reality? For if, according to you, the sprout here were non-different from the seed, [it would follow that they are identical]. (6.10)

For it could not be grasped at all, like a seed [grasped] as what is called a sprout; or else, even that [seed] might be grasped [as the sprout], since these two would be identical in reality. Therefore, this [identity] must not be accepted. (6.11)
Furthermore, the world does not accept the identity of these two,
since it perceives the fruit even when the cause has perished;
therefore, this [identity] exists neither in reality nor according to worldly convention.
It is logical to conceive that an entity arises from itself;
for if arising were held to be from self, it would apply to the produced, the producer, the action, and the agent. (6.12)
Nor should it be accepted that there is neither identity nor non-identity between these two, because birth would then be subject to the faults inherent in its own nature.
If the other were to exist in dependence upon something else... [6.13]
In that case, there would be abundant darkness even from a flame;
moreover, everything would indeed arise from everything, because "otherness" is equal in respect to all things, including those that are not the producer. (6.14)
Therefore, that which is capable of being produced is defined as the "effect" (*kārya*);
thus, even a remote cause is one that is capable of its production,
as is a proximate producer belonging to the same single continuum.
And if it is not so from barley and the like regarding the shoot of rice,
then [the cause] is not accepted as being a producer, nor as possessing the capacity,
nor as belonging to the same continuum, nor even as being similar.
The sprout of rice is not the barley, the kesar, the kiṃśuka, and so forth, nor even its own seed, because it is other than them;
and yet the sprout does not exist at the same time as the seed.
How could there be a seed without otherness?
For the birth of the sprout from the seed is not established by way of otherness; therefore, let the position that it arises from another be abandoned. (6.17)
Just as the lowering and raising of the two ends of a balance scale are certainly not observed to occur at the same time,
so too it is with the cessation of the producer and the birth of the produced.
If that [entity] were non-existent at one time, it could not exist here without [changing its] time;
if this [entity] facing birth were not existent,
then even that which is being destroyed while facing destruction would not be existent.
In that case, how could this [eye] be equal to it on the scale?
Furthermore, without an agent, this production is not logical.
Indeed, the visual consciousness [is produced] by its own generators, namely the eye and so forth.

If there is distinctness [of the entity] from its coexistent factors such as perception and so forth, which exist at the same time, what is the purpose of its production? For if it already exists, it cannot be brought into being; or if it does not exist, the fault has already been established in that case. (6.20)
If a producer were to produce another thing that is to be produced, would that cause be existent, non-existent, both, or devoid of both?
(3) If it is existent, what need has it of producers; and if it is non-existent, what use is there for them?
Even if duality exists, what is gained by them? Or if duality has vanished, what is gained by them?
What indeed could be accomplished here by this described reasoning, since the world is held to be a valid authority when it remains within its own perspective?

And since the world indeed passes from one state to another state, what is the need for a further rebirth here, given that its existence is already obtained through correct or false perception? (6.22) [That which has acquired its being through correct or false perception...]
All entities possess two natures:
that which is the object for those with correct vision is reality (*tattva*); that which is the object for those with false vision is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). (6.23)
For even false perception is considered to be of two kinds: that with clear faculties and that with impaired faculties;
[the latter] is false in relation to cognition produced by healthy faculties.
Knowledge is considered to be defective when there is injury to the sense organs.
That which the world perceives as graspable by all six sense organs occurs only in the absence of such injury.

For that which is real is indeed [known] from the world itself; the rest is conceptualized, and what is false is known from the world itself. (6.25) By those who are nodding in the sleep of ignorance...
Those [entities] which are conceived by various philosophical schools according to their own systems,
as well as those imagined in relation to illusions, mirages, and the like—
their lack of ultimate reality is indeed evident even from the perspective of worldly convention. (6.26)

Just as the perception of those with cataracts is not sublated for those without cataracts, so too [the perception] of those who are obscured by impure knowledge [is not sublated] for those whose vision is purified by stainless knowledge.
There is no sublation by cognition, for cognition is stainless.
Delusion is the concealer because it obscures the true nature; that which appears as real through it is merely artificial.

That sage declared that to be conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*); for the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) consists of produced things and conceptualized objects arising through the power of cataracts. (6.28)
That very form of hair and so forth is false;
that by which one with pure vision perceives it is reality—understand it thus here as well. (6.29)
If the world were the authority because it perceives reality, then the world alone would suffice; what need would there be for other Noble Ones?
And what purpose would be served by the Noble Path?

For it is certainly not logical that a fool should be an authority. (6.30) Therefore, the world is not an authority in every respect; thus, in the matter of ultimate reality, there is no contradiction with worldly consensus.
There would be a contradiction with worldly experience if a worldly object were refuted by mere worldly consensus; for the world, indeed, even after sowing, [reaps] merely the seed. 6.31.
"This son has been begotten by me," he says; yet since the tree that was planted has gone elsewhere, it does not even belong to him according to worldly convention. (6.32)
Since the sprout is not other than the seed, when the sprout exists, the seed has therefore not perished;
since they are not one, for that reason also the seed [is not destroyed].

If it exists as a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) dependent [on causes], then when that [characteristic] is negated, the entity itself would perish; therefore, one must certainly not say "it exists" regarding the sprout. 6.33
It might be argued that emptiness is the cause for the destruction of entities;
this is not logical, for because of it, no entity exists.
These [entities] do not exist prior to their acquisition of a nature consisting of reality.
When things are being investigated, they find no stability; therefore, one should not apply investigation to the conventional truth of worldly affairs. (6.35)
For in the section on reality (*tattva*), by the very same reasoning through which birth from oneself or from another is shown to be illogical,
by that same reasoning it is [illogical] even from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
It is not logical; by what means could your birth occur? (6.36) Empty things such as reflections and the like, which depend upon a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), are certainly not unestablished. (5)
And just as the mind arises from an empty reflection and the like, assuming its form,
so too indeed are all phenomena empty.
They arise from nothing but emptiness;
they are neither annihilated nor eternal, because by nature there is an absence [of intrinsic being] even within the two truths. (6.38)
Because it is not ceased by its own nature,
even after an action has been ceased for a long time,
its power [remains] in some cases even without a storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
"Understand that the fruit arises [from this].
Just as there is attachment for a fool even upon waking to objects perceived in a dream, so too is it with this.
In the same way, a fruit arises from an action that has ceased and possesses a non-existent nature;
this is just as [an object is perceived] despite the object being equally non-existent.
One suffering from ophthalmia perceives the form of hair;
understand that it does not perceive the forms of all things.
Likewise, once [karma] has ripened, there is no further ripening. (6.41)
For from this black [karma] an inauspicious ripening is seen, and from the auspicious, an auspicious ripening alone;
and liberation results from the cognition of the non-existence of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
"There is a prohibition against anxiety regarding the fruits of actions" (6.42).
For this teaching is intended for one who does not understand such extremely profound subjects.
There exists the storehouse-consciousness (ālaya), and there indeed exists the person (pudgala), or else these aggregates (skandhas) alone; just as he taught [the notions] "I" and "mine. 6.43a-b.
Even though the view of a self-identity has vanished, the Buddha taught that all phenomena exist— though they lack intrinsic nature— by way of provisional meaning. (6.44)
For that bodhisattva dwelling in wisdom has penetrated the reality of consciousness-only;
seeing no subject of grasping in the absence of an object of grasping.
The three realms of existence are nothing but consciousness.
Just as waves arise from the great ocean through the impelling force of the wind, [so do the worlds arise from consciousness].
Likewise, from that which is called the storehouse (ālaya), which contains all seeds, there arises mere consciousness through its own power; therefore,
the dependent nature exists.

That which arises as an external object of apprehension, though it is based on a thing that exists only as a conceptual designation, is itself real and has a nature that is not an object for any conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). (6.47)
If it is argued that the mind exists even without anything external,
just as in a dream, then this very point must be considered:
for even in a dream, I do not possess a mind at all.
Whenever that is so, there is no illustration for you [to cite].
If the mind exists because of the recollection of a dream upon waking, let it be; likewise, let there also be an external object.

"Just as there is memory for you that 'it was seen by me,' so too is the occurrence of memory possible regarding external objects. (6.49) [This occurs] when there is the very occurrence of visual cognition during sleep.
The mind indeed exists, yet it is purely mental;
if you think that its placement as something external within its own form is just as it is here [in waking life] as it is in a dream, then [we reply]: 6.50.
Just as those external objects were not produced for you, so too the mind was not produced in the dream;
nor were the eye, the object of the eye, or that which arises from them.
And the mind— all three are likewise unreal.
(6.51) Just as the remaining three, beginning with the ear, are unarisen in a dream, so too are they unarisen here in the waking state.
All things are false; that mind does not exist, nor its object-field, nor do the sense-faculties exist—so long as one has not attained awakening.
(6.52) As long as one does not attain realization, [they] exist.
For these three exist for him here only so long as there is no awakening; yet when awakening occurs, even those three become unreal,
just as they do upon the exhaustion of the sleep of delusion.
That which has the form of hair, which a person with diseased eyes perceives through a certain cognition due to the power of *timira* (ophthalmia)—
both of these are real in relation to that cognition.
For one who perceives the clear reality, both are false.
(6.54) If indeed cognition could exist without an object of knowledge, it would belong to one whose eyes are directed toward the place of [illusory] hair.
Furthermore, even for one whose cataracts have been removed, the perception of [non-existent] hair would still occur;
however, it does not happen in this way. Therefore, this is not the case.
There is no impairment of the power of the intellect for one who possesses pure vision.
For that reason, no cognition arises for him;
if it is argued that this is not so because of the absence of the existence of an object of knowledge, [we reply] that it is not established, because of the absence of its capacity. (6.56)
For that which has already arisen, there is no possibility of power; nor does that which has not yet arisen possess power.
There is no qualifier without a qualified object.
Furthermore, this consequence would apply even to the son of a barren woman.
If you maintain that the designation is based on what is yet to be, there is no such "future-ness" for him without an underlying capacity.
The wise declare that a proof which depends upon mutual reliance is indeed no proof at all. [And] from the ripening of obstructed power, it would come to be... 6.58
If the arising of another were from a different power, there would be a mutual distinction among the members of the continuum; consequently, everything would arise from everything. (6.59)
Even though the possessors of the continuum (*santānin*) are distinct therein,
there is indeed no difference in their continuum;
therefore, it is to be established that there is no fault.
Because it is illogical for there to be a continuity of non-difference [between them].
For the dharmas residing in Maitreya and Upagupta do not belong to a single continuum, because they are distinct entities.
Even those [moments] which are distinct according to their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) are not logically possible as belonging to a single continuum,
since the arising of visual cognition occurs from its own potential (svaśakti).
Immediately following that capacity,
which is the support for its own consciousness, there arises the cognition of the material sense-faculty as "the eye. (6.62)
Not realizing that here consciousness arises from its own seeds, manifesting as blue and so forth, without an external form, and originating from the eye;
People perceive the external object as being distinct from the mind;
yet, just as in a dream, the mind arises in the form of an object even without any external thing existing apart from it.

If the mind arises here even for one who is awake, without an external object, due to the ripening of its own potential, then the consciousness manifests as the appearance of blue and so forth. (6.64)
Just as in a dream the mental [cognition] occurs even in the absence of the eyes,
why does it not likewise arise here for a blind person upon the loss of the eyes, through the ripening of its own seed? (6.65)
If you should think that the ripening of the sixth [sense] occurs in a dream but not while awake,
then just as there is no ripening of the sixth sense here [in the waking state], so it is elsewhere.
Do you not know that it is likewise present in a dream?
Just as the absence of eyes is not the cause for this [visual perception] even in a dream, so too torpor (*middha*) is not the cause.
Therefore, one must admit that even in a dream, the eye has that same nature; it is the cause for the cognition of an unreal object.
Whatever refutation this [opponent] may offer—
Seeing each of these as equivalent to his own thesis, one should refrain from such debate; for the Buddhas do not maintain that any entity whatsoever exists as a real thing. (6.68)
Even when a yogi, through the instruction of a guru, comprehends the entire earth by means of mental resolve,
he should perceive therein that even these three are unborn.

Because it is taught as being due to false mental attention (mithyāmanaskāra). As you hold that there is the form of the object in the cognition of the eye, so it would be for the mind in the [contemplation of] the foul (aśubhā).
In that case, for another person who perceives that same place, there would likewise be cognition [of water],
and that cognition would not be false;
yet, even when water is flowing, one may have the cognition of pus.
To a hungry ghost, it is like the waters of a river appearing as darkness; in brief, understand this point: that just as the object does not exist, so too the cognition does not exist. 6.71
If the dependent nature— which is devoid of a grasped object and separated from the state of a grasper, and empty of duality—
exists, by what means do you seek its existence?
And it is illogical to say that what is not being apprehended exists;
therefore, its experience by that very [consciousness] is not established.
If it is argued that it is established by memory at a later time, [we reply:]
This unestablished [reason], being explained for the sake of establishing what is unestablished, certainly cannot serve as a proof.
Let it be granted that self-cognition is established.

Nevertheless, it is not logical for the knower to be [identical with] memory, because, like the continuum of ignorance, he is distinct; furthermore, this [reasoning] would also destroy specific distinctions. (6.74)
Since the object was experienced by that [self], there is no otherness for this rememberer;
because of this, the memory "I saw it" would occur.
And this is the principle of worldly convention.
Therefore, self-cognition exists; for you, there could never be the apprehension of anything else through another means.
There is no identity between the agent, the action, and the object;
therefore, it is not logical for that [agent] to apprehend itself. (6.76) Even that which is unarisen has an undiscernible nature.
If existence were of the nature of the dependent,
what harm could the son of a barren woman possibly do to another, such that one would not perceive his reality? (6.77)
When no other tantra exists at all,
what indeed would be the basis for conventional [truths]?
Those ruined by greed for another's property—
All established conventions are also proven by the world.
6.78 For those who have gone outside the path of the venerable teacher Nāgārjuna, there is no means to attain auspiciousness.
For they have fallen away from the truth of conventional reality;
and due to that fall, there is no accomplishment of liberation. (6.79) Conventional reality is the means.
The ultimate truth is that which constitutes the goal;
he who does not discern the distinction between these two through false conceptualizations has indeed entered upon a wrong path. 6.80
Nor have I accepted conventional reality in the form of the dependent nature as you desire; rather,
it is said to be "non-existent" for those [fools] merely out of conformity with worldly convention.
"I say 'it exists' for the sake of the goal to be accomplished.
Just as there is no such thing as 'worthiness' when one has cast off the aggregates and entered into Śiva, so too [the self] would not exist."
If I were to say that this [self] exists in the same way as the world does, then it would certainly not be established even from the perspective of the world;
indeed, it should be refuted by the world itself.
There would be no contradiction with the world for you if it were so; let the world and your honor debate this here, and afterwards I shall take refuge with the stronger side. (6.83)
The Bodhisattva, being present in the stage of Presence, realizes that the three realms of existence are mere consciousness,
through the awakening that negates the notions of permanence, a self, and a creator.

The agent enters into that which is mind-only. Therefore, for the sake of increasing the wisdom of the wise, it was spoken by the Omniscient One, who shatters the lofty mountains of rival teachers. (6.84) (11)
In that *Ārya-Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, regarding the cessation of the twilight [of ignorance], this collection of speech is the vajra;
these [teachings] are described in various treatises.

Just as the non-Buddhists, through their own reasoning, perceive the person and so forth as the agent according to their respective views, the Jina taught to the world that "mind alone" is the agent. (6.86)
Just as the Buddha is etymologically defined as the reality of awakening, so too the world is said in the Sūtra to be primarily mind-only;
"mind-only" is stated there as a negation [of external objects].
The meaning of the sutra here is thus: "not of form.
If only form is negated there, having understood that "this is mind-only," [then form is not denied].
The Great-Souled One spoke again regarding why the mind here is born from the karma of delusion,
concerning both the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world.
The mind alone creates the most diverse [world];
for it is said that the entire world is born of karma, and apart from the mind, karma does not exist. (6.89)
Although form indeed exists,
it does not possess agency as the mind does;
therefore, [agency] belongs to the other, namely the mind.
Indeed, the negation of form is not a prohibition;
for these five aggregates, well-known in the world, exist for one who abides in worldly reality.
When the arising of the knowledge of reality is desired,
these five indeed do not arise for yogins at all.
In the absence of form, do not grasp at the existence of the mind.

Do not fall into the view that there is an absence of form or that the mind is a sentient being; for in the Sūtras, these two are understood through wisdom to be the same, and they are both rejected and described by the Buddhas in the Abhidharma. (6.92)
Even by breaking this sequence of the two truths, those entities do not attain established existence, for that is prohibited.
Therefore, understand all things through such a method.

Those born in the world and those who are in truth unborn from the beginning; and as it is stated in the Sūtra: "Indeed, there is no external object of perception; rather, it is the mind itself that appears in various forms. (6.93)
"Those who are excessively attached to form—bind that form for them. This is of interpretable meaning (neyārtha); and the Teacher declared its state of being interpretable.
Moreover, this scripture demonstrates that this sūtra, as well as other sūtras of a similar kind, is of interpretable meaning (neyārtha) through logical reasoning. 6.95
The Buddhas declare that the negation of cognition can be easily attained without [first negating] the object of cognition; therefore,
they teach the negation of the object of cognition first.
Because when the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) does not exist, the negation of knowledge (*jñāna*) is established.
(6.96) Having thus understood the system of the scripture, that which was stated as having a provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) for the sake of exposition—
Having understood the sūtra, let that which is not definitive be set aside,
and let the meaning of emptiness be known as the definitive meaning.
Furthermore, production from two [causes] is certainly not logical.
For faults fall upon those very [theories] that have been proposed;
this is not desired either by common worldly consensus or from the perspective of ultimate reality, since the production of a being cannot be established through any one of them alone. (6.98)
If birth were to occur even without a cause, then everything would arise from everything at all times,
just as hundreds of fruits might be produced from seeds and the like.
Furthermore, the world would certainly not engage in gathering [things together],
nor would the universe ever be perceived if it were devoid of causes,
just like the color and fragrance of a lotus in the sky.
You perceive the world as something exceedingly variegated; therefore,
abandon that world like your own conceptualization arising from a cause,
for those elements do not possess such a nature.
By whatever nature your cognitions become objects, within that very [nature] there is a dense darkness of mind; how then will he properly reach the supreme world? 6.101 (13)
O you who hold a view contrary to the true nature of the knowable, understand yourself as being "another" at the time of denying the next world;
for you possess a body that serves as a basis similar to that produced by such a view.
When you attain the existence of the self composed of the elements, it is at that very moment;
for those elements do not exist in the manner they have been described in general terms.
Arising from self, from another, or from both, as well as arising without a cause—these have indeed been refuted previously;
therefore, these elements do not exist when they have not arisen. (6.103)
Since phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, and since there is no arising from self, from another, or from both, nor indeed without depending on a cause;
therefore, delusion is thick, like a dense mass of clouds.
By that [ignorance], the objects of the world indeed appear falsely,
just as someone, through the power of ophthalmia, perceives such things as hair, a second moon, a peacock’s tail-feathers, or flies, though they are unreal.
In the same way, the ignorant person indeed perceives the diverse conditioned world through their intellect due to the fault of delusion.
If karma exists dependent upon delusion, it does not exist without delusion.
"Only the ignorant person indeed goes to ruin by thinking 'that is real';
for he is shrouded in dense darkness deprived of the sun of right understanding.
But the wise person understands it to be empty and is liberated. (6.106)
If indeed things do not exist in reality,
then their non-existence would follow even from the perspective of conventional discourse,
just like that of the son of a barren woman.
Therefore, they exist by way of their own intrinsic nature.
For those hairs and so forth which, being produced from a visual disorder such as *taimira*, become objects [of perception], do not exist at all.

Indeed, those very things are first to be questioned, and subsequently [examined] as they arise from the cataract of ignorance: a dream, a city of Gandharvas, and a mirage. (6.108) svapnaṃ sagandharvapuraṃ marīcyām...
If you perceive things such as Indra’s net or reflections as being unarisen, how can that be? For it is not tenable, since they are equal in their lack of existence. (6.109)
These things do not exist in reality as they have arisen, nor do they cease like the son of a barren woman;
yet they come within the range of perception for the world.
Therefore, what was stated is inconclusive. (6.110) Birth does not exist in reality even for the son of a barren woman, let alone from a worldly perspective.
Thus, by their own nature, all these entities are neither born from the perspective of the world nor in terms of ultimate reality;
he taught that phenomena have been quiescent from the very beginning.
Therefore, since the Teacher has declared that all things are by nature extinguished and free from arising, there is consequently no such thing as truly existent birth. (6.112)
These things, such as jars and the like, do not exist in reality; however, just as they appear through worldly convention,
so shall all phenomena come to be.

There would not be the consequence [of non-arising] like that of the son of a barren woman, because [arising] occurs without a cause, from a cause such as Īśvara, from itself, from another, or from both. 6.113a–b.
From whatever [cause], whether from itself, from another, or from both, [there is no arising].
For entities do not exist while they are arising;
therefore, they proceed as originating dependently.
By means of this dependent origination of entities, [liberation] is possible.
Since these conceptual constructions cannot be conceptually constructed,
this principle of dependent origination cuts through the entire web of false views. 6.115
Conceptual constructions may exist when a thing is present;
however, one must examine how that thing does not exist,
just as there is no fire without fuel.
In the same way, these [conceptual constructions] do not exist without an object.
The wise declare that the cessation of conceptual constructions is the fruit of inquiry.
Ordinary people are bound by conceptualization alone;
the yogi who does not conceptualize attains liberation.
This investigation was not undertaken out of a desire for debate. (6.117)
But the reality taught in the scripture is for the sake of liberation. Even if other systems have come to diverge when that reality is being explained, there is no fault. 6.118

For attachment to one's own view is indeed a mere conceptual construction, as is the anger felt toward another's view; therefore, having shaken off both attachment and aversion, [one should remain equanimous]. (15)
By investigating with wisdom, one perceives all afflictions and defects without exception as arising from the view of a self-identity, and thus swiftly attains liberation.
Having understood both the self and its object,
the yogi effects the negation of the self alone. (6.120) The self is conceptualized by the non-Buddhists as being eternal in nature.
"The agent and enjoyer is devoid of qualities and inactive; the various systems of the non-Buddhists have come to differentiate him by relying on this or that distinction. (6.121)
For a self of such a nature, there is no existence; therefore,
it is not logical for this to be the basis of the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), because it is devoid of birth, like the son of a barren woman.
Even conventionally, its existence is not accepted.
Those specific qualities of it which are pointed out by the non-Buddhists in various treatises, the reason for those is its non-arising.
Since that which is established by itself subverts all [other positions], therefore not all its specific features exist either;
thus, no self exists as something other than the aggregates. (6.123)

Having abandoned the aggregates, because the grasping for them is not established, even the world does not accept a basis for the notion of "I," since the view of self belongs to those who do not know that [reality]. (6.124)
Even those who have increased through eons as animals do not see him, for they are perpetually unborn; yet,
having seen him, even their sense of egoism ceases.
Therefore, there is no self whatsoever other than the aggregates (skandhas). Indeed,
the aggregates alone are the objective support for the view of a self, because no self established as distinct from the aggregates exists.

Some maintain that all five aggregates are the self, while others hold that it is the mind alone which serves as the basis for the view of self. If the aggregates were the self, then [the self] would be multiple because of their multiplicity.
In this way, those selves would also become numerous;
furthermore, the self would result in being a substance, and there would be no reversal in its occurrence within that substance. (6.127)
One would necessarily be a self-annihilator upon entering nirvāṇa,
and there would be destruction and arising during the moments prior to nirvāṇa;
because of the destruction of the agent, there would likewise be an absence of its fruit.
One would enjoy the karma earned by another;
there would be no fault if the continuum were real,
for the fault regarding the continuum was already stated in the previous investigation.
The aggregates are neither the self nor the mind; therefore,
because there is no end to this world and so forth, for the yogi who perceives the non-existence of a self— 6.129.

Then there would necessarily be both existence and non-existence for you; if the eternal self is rejected by you at that time, then it must be either the aggregates or the mind, and therefore it is not a self. (6.130)
For a yogin who perceives the non-existence of a self, the true nature of form and the other [objects] would not be reached,
because [the mind] functions by taking the form of passion and so forth as its object.
There might be [the notion of] arising from a failure to understand its true nature.
(6.131) If it is held that because the Teacher stated "the aggregates are the self," the aggregates themselves are therefore considered the self; [then...]

This is a negation of a self distinct from the aggregates, because it is stated in another sūtra, such as "form is not the self," and so forth: "Form is not the self; neither is sensation, nor is perception.
(6.132) Form is not the self; sensation is not, nor is perception.
Neither formations nor consciousness are mentioned [as the self] in another sutra; therefore, the teaching of the sutra is that the aggregates alone are not accepted as the self. (6.133)
If it is said that the aggregates are the self, then the self would be a mere collection of aggregates and not the nature of the aggregates themselves;
it would possess neither lordship, nor self-control, nor witnesshood.
Because that [collection] does not exist, there can therefore be no aggregate. At that time, immovable things would possess the nature of a chariot;
thus, the self-nature of its parts would be identical to that of the chariot. (6.134) (17)
And since it is explained in the Sūtra with reference to the aggregates,
the self is therefore not merely the collection of the aggregates.
If [it is argued that] it is the shape of material things, then [the self would be non-existent], because that [shape] exists [only for material things].

The notion that "these very [aggregates] are the self" might occur to you; however, the collection of mind and so forth cannot be the self, because they possess no structural configuration (saṃniveśa). (6.136)
It is not logical for the appropriator to be one with its own appropriated [aggregates]; likewise, there would be an identity between agent and action.
If you think that the agent exists while the action does not, [that too is untenable].
For there is no action without an agent. Depending upon earth, water, fire, air, consciousness, and space— || 6.137 ||
The Sage taught that the self consists of six elements,
namely the six bases of contact beginning with the eye, and it also consists of the mental states and mental factors derived from those phenomena.
Since it is designated by means of them, it is not their true nature;
nor is it a mere aggregate of them.
Therefore, the notion of "I" does not apply to those [elements]. (6.139)
The eternal self is discarded when there is the realization of non-self,
and this [self] is not accepted as the basis for the notion of "I.
For one who knows the absence of a self, how could that [notion of "I"] arise from their own view?
And it is said that he was "uprooted"— this is truly marvelous!
Seeing a snake in a hole in his own house, the elephant here, free from all suspicion, thought, "The snake is not there."
He abandons even the fear of a serpent— oh,
how great indeed is his uprightness toward another!
For the self does not exist within these aggregates (skandhas), nor do they [exist] in it.
Since it is not the case here that "the aggregates exist in the self," this conceptual construction could indeed occur if there were a state of otherness;
however, since that otherness does not exist, this is merely a conceptual construction. (6.142)
The self is not desired as something possessing form, because no self exists; for there is no connection with a possessive suffix [matvarthīya] here.
Indeed, [the suffix occurs] when there is difference, as in "one who possesses cows" (gomān), and also when there is non-difference, as in "possessing form" (rūpavān). (18)
The self does not exist as identical to or different from form (rūpa).
Form is not the self, nor is the self possessed of form;
the self is not in form, nor is form in the self, for it is non-existent [therein].
Know all the aggregates (skandhas) in this way; these twenty-four parts are held by one's own view.
These are those peaks that have arisen.
Established upon the vast mountain of the view of a self-identity,
when the self is split open by the vajra that awakens one to selflessness, that mountain of views also goes to destruction along with it. (6.145)
Some maintain that the person (pudgala) exists as a substantial reality, which cannot be described as either identical to or different from [the aggregates], nor as permanent or impermanent;
they further assert that it is cognizable by the six consciousnesses.
Thus, it is accepted that this [basis] is the support for the notion of "I.
Nor is it inexpressible; for that which is perceived as a real entity cannot be rendered inexpressible by way of its form, as is the case with the mind.

If some self were established as a real entity, it would not be inexpressible, for its nature would be established just like that of the mind. As for that self which has been declared inexpressible in relation to the aggregates—

Do not go [to the conclusion] that the *sattva* is established by its own nature; for if it were unestablished as a real entity (*vastu*), your pot would consequently become inexpressible in relation to form and the other [sensory qualities]. (6.148)
Your consciousness is held to be non-different from its own self,
yet it is considered to be of a different nature from form and the other [objects].
These two paths regarding a real entity are indeed observed.

There is no self because it is devoid of the properties of real entities (6.149). Therefore, the basis of the ego-conception is not a real entity; it is neither other than the aggregates nor does it have the nature of the aggregates.
The self is neither the support of the aggregates, nor is it the possessor of them;
rather, having appropriated the aggregates, it attains its established state.
Just as a chariot is not considered something other than its own parts, [so too is the self not distinct from the aggregates].
Nor is it non-different from them, nor indeed does it possess them;
it is not in the parts, nor are the parts in it, nor is it the mere collection, nor is it the configuration. (6.151)
For if a chariot were merely its collection [of parts], then the state of being a chariot would exist even in those parts while they remain stationary;
and it is not logical that a chariot is merely its configuration.
Since there are no parts that exist apart from the possessor of parts,
just as the configuration previously existed in the individual parts, so too does it exist when they have come together to form a chariot.
If it were exactly so, then even now there would be no chariot,
just as there was none when those constituent elements were disjoined; yet, if there is a difference in configuration now, [then the chariot exists].

If it were so, then at the time when the wheels and other parts constitute a chariot, this [chariot] would have to be perceived; yet this is not the case, for there is no chariot apart from the mere configuration. Therefore, [the chariot does not exist]. (6.154)
Nor is that configuration of the collection of parts yours; for the collection is nothing at all,
so how indeed could that which is not anything at all exist?
"In this case, it will exist by depending on configuration;
just as you have desired, so it is, by relying upon a cause that is itself unreal. (6.155)

"Understand that indeed every collection of effects arises while being devoid of intrinsic nature; by this [same reasoning], the cognition of a jar regarding form and so forth [is explained]. 6.156. By this, [the cognition of a jar regarding] form and so forth...

It is likewise not at all logical to say that they exist in such a state; for form and the other [sensory objects] do not exist when unarisen, and therefore their configuration is also not logical. (6.157)
Although it does not achieve establishment in seven ways either from the perspective of ultimate reality or from the perspective of the world,
it nonetheless proceeds [as such] by taking its own parts as its basis, without analysis.
And this [chariot] is designated from the perspective of worldly convention alone.
For among people, there is the common usage: "That very thing is the constituent part; that is the whole; that is the agent; that is the chariot. (6.158)

Even though you are established as the appropriator of people, do not destroy the worldly convention that is established by the world. How indeed could that which does not exist in seven ways be [established]? 6.159 (20)
Thus, the yogin does not attain existence [as an ordinary being]; let it be accepted that even the entry into reality occurs with ease—such is his accomplishment here. (6.160)
If the self does not exist as the chariot at that time,
then its constituent parts do not exist either without the possessor of the body; just as when a chariot is burnt, its parts no longer exist [as such].
Just as a limb [is consumed] when the body is burnt by the fire of the intellect,
so too is the self (ātman) accepted as the appropriator,
having appropriated the aggregates (skandhas) according to worldly convention.
Likewise, the elements and the six sense-bases, as well as karma and grasping, and he who is the agent—
therein is neither impermanence nor permanence. (6.162)
This [self] is neither born nor does it perish;
neither permanence nor the like exists for it, nor is there any otherness, because it lacks substantial existence. (6.163)
This is that Self in whom the notion of "I" has always proceeded for the worlds,
and in whom there is the cognition of "mine."
It arises from delusion through a mind that does not investigate;
for there is no action without an agent, and therefore, without a self and what belongs to a self, [the notion of "mine"] is non-existent.
Thus, seeing the self and that which belongs to the self as empty, the yogi attains liberation.
(6.165) A pot, a cloth, a mat, an army, a forest, a row of trees—

Understand that whatever objects there may be— such as houses, carts, monasteries, and so forth— by means of which people conduct their worldly affairs, it is regarding these that the Lord of Sages does not dispute with the world. (6.166)

The qualities of the parts, such as redness, are the *lakṣaṇas* (characteristics), while the objects such as fire, which are colored by the qualities of the whole, are the *lakṣya* (the characterized).
Through the investigation of the chariot already set forth, these do not exist in seven ways.

But if that other [the effect] exists, they exist by way of worldly convention. (6.167) If the cause produces only that which is to be produced, then it does not produce an effect; for if it were without that [effect], it would be causeless.
Even when a cause exists, the fruit arises from it; therefore, tell me: what could exist beforehand, and from what could it arise? 6.168 (21)
If the cause produces the effect only after reaching it, then there would be no distinction between the producer and the fruit, because of their identity in power.
Furthermore, this cause would be indistinguishable from non-causes.
Having discarded this pair, there is another false conceptualization:
"Now, since your cause does not produce an effect, the effect is non-existent; therefore, being devoid of an effect and lacking a cause, it is not a cause. (6.169)
Even this dyad is like an illusion;
therefore, no fault attaches to me, for worldly objects do exist. Having encountered this refutation, it refutes that which is to be refuted.

"Is it not the case that this fault applies to you as well, since you say 'without having reached'? When you speak in this way, you destroy your own position; at that time, you are certainly not capable of refuting [the opponent]. (6.171)
By means of various sophistical arguments that apply equally even to your own words, you refute all categories of reality in the absence of valid reasoning;
therefore, indeed, you are not esteemed by the virtuous.

And since you are a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), you have no position of your own. For you have no fixed position such that your refutation necessarily either fails to reach its object or reaches the object to be refuted.
This fault might arise for him; however, this position—that [the self] does not exist—is not a contingency that applies to me.
For you have observed these specific qualities in the act of grasping and so forth.
The solar discs are present both in the actual orb and in the reflection; yet it is not logical for the reflection to arise without reaching the sun, nor can it exist by reaching it.
Thus, it exists only through dependence and is a mere conventional designation.

Just as that which is false may nonetheless serve to produce the adornment of one's own face, so too should you understand this case here: that [the reason] resides in its own probandum despite being devoid of logical justification.
For one who has observed its efficacy regarding the construction of the gateway of wisdom,

if there were indeed a reason established by the nature of things (*vastusiddha*) that leads through the application of logical principles such as attainment, it would certainly be a means of proving its own probandum. (6.175) (22)
Even the nature of the probandum must be understood through actual entities;
since that does not exist for you, there is only exhaustion. [It is impossible] to make all categories of objects understood when they are devoid of any real basis.
The world can be awakened by one who is capable with ease, yet its inherent nature is not so easily overcome; how much less, then, can it be subdued here by the web of futile reasoning? (6.177)
Having understood the remaining refutations previously taught for the purpose of abandoning the positions such as "attainment" (prāpti) and so forth, apply them here; furthermore,
it has been stated how even the status of a caviller (vaitaṇḍika) does not exist.
Understand the remainder by this very same method.
This twofold selflessness has been explained through the distinction between phenomena (*dharma*) and the person (*ātman*), for the sake of the world's liberation.

Having broken that very [teaching] into many parts once again, the Teacher spoke thus to those to be trained: having briefly explained the sixteen kinds of emptiness along with their conceptual elaborations. (6.179)
Furthermore, four [emptinesses] are proclaimed, and they are considered to be in the Mahāyāna as well:
the eye is indeed empty of the eye, because such is its intrinsic nature;
likewise for the ear, mind, tongue, nose, and body.
It is said:
"The lack of intrinsic nature (asvabhāvatā) of the six [faculties], beginning with the eye, based on their being neither immutable nor subject to destruction, is what is intended. 6.181
Internal emptiness:
Form is indeed empty of form, because that is its very nature.
Likewise are sounds, tastes, smells, mental phenomena, and tangibles.
And: 6.183 The absence of intrinsic nature in form and so forth is considered external emptiness;
the absence of intrinsic nature in both is internal-external emptiness. 6.184 (23)
The absence of intrinsic nature in phenomena is called "emptiness" by the wise;
and that emptiness itself is empty, for it is considered to have the very form of emptiness. (6.185)
That which is called emptiness is considered the emptiness of emptiness;

it is taught as the emptiness of the notions of existence in order to eliminate grasping. (6.186) Because it pervades the world of sentient beings and the receptacle-world without exception, [it is so designated].
Because there is no limit to the directions, they are immeasurable;
their vastness is due to the directions themselves, yet even these ten directions are empty.
That which is called "great emptiness" is taught for the sake of ceasing the great grasping.
For the ultimate truth is nirvāṇa; this is the supreme goal.
Its emptiness is, therefore, the emptiness of the ultimate. [This is taught] in order to eliminate the grasping at existence regarding those who conceive of nirvāṇa as a real entity. 6.189
Emptiness, which is the ultimate reality, has been taught by those who know the supreme truth. Indeed, the three realms are explained as being conditioned, arising from causal conditions.

That which is the emptiness of that [conditioned] is called by him the "emptiness of the conditioned. That which is the emptiness of that which is unconditioned— namely, that which does not possess these [characteristics of] arising, abiding, and impermanence—
is called by him the "emptiness of the unconditioned."
That which has no end is called "absolute" (*atyanta*);
its emptiness by virtue of that very [endlessness] is described as "absolute emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). (6.193)

The beginning is the "lower," and the end is the "upper"; by the absence of these, it is described as such. For *saṃsāra* is indeed without lower or upper limit, due to the separation from coming and going. That which is the state of this dream-like existence being devoid of that very [coming and going]— 6.194. The beginning is the lower, and the end is the upper; by the absence of those, it is so described. For *saṃsāra* is indeed without lower or upper limit, because of the cessation of coming and going.
That which is the state of this dream-like existence being separated from that very [coming and going]—
This is explained in the treatise as "emptiness without rejection" (śūnyatānavarāgra).
"Rejection" (avakāra) is defined as scattering, dispersing, or casting away;
however, "non-rejection" (anavarāgra) is not a casting away that is abandoned.
Because there is no room for anything whatsoever,
that very emptiness of it is called "the emptiness of non-exclusion"; therefore,
this is so designated.
Since the intrinsic nature of conditioned phenomena and so forth was not created by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, or Tathāgatas, [it is therefore uncreated]. (6.198)
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of conditioned phenomena and so forth is described as their "nature" (*prakṛti*).

That which is the emptiness of that very [nature] is what is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). (6.199) The eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the six types of contact (*sparśa*), and the six feelings (*vedanā*) born thereof;
Formed and formless phenomena, as well as conditioned and unconditioned ones—whatever is the emptiness of all these phenomena, which is their being devoid of those [respective] characteristics;
that which is the absence of deformation and so forth is the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*). (6.200–201)
Form has the characteristic of being subject to transformation; feeling consists of experience;
perception is the grasping of signs; while formations are volitional construction.
The specific characteristic of consciousness is the representation of each respective object.
The aggregates have suffering as their specific characteristic; the elements are considered to be like venomous serpents;
and the sense-bases were taught by the Buddhas as the gateways for the influx [of experience]. (6.203)

That which is dependent origination has the specific characteristic of being a causal complex. (6.204) The perfection of generosity is relinquishment; ethical discipline has the characteristic of non-burning; patience has the characteristic of non-anger; while vigor consists in faultlessness. (6.205)
Meditative concentration has the characteristic of gathering, and wisdom has the characteristic of non-attachment;
indeed, this is declared to be the characteristic of the six perfections. (6.206)
The meditative absorptions (dhyānas), the immeasurables (apramāṇas), and likewise the other formless attainments (ārūpyas)—
these have been described by the one who possesses perfect knowledge as having the characteristic of non-agitation.
The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣyas) have the specific characteristic of leading to liberation.
The characteristic of emptiness is solitude, because there is no apprehension.
The characteristic of the signless is peace; however, the characteristic of the third [liberation] is liberation from suffering and delusion. 6.208–209
The powers are said to be of a well-ascertained nature,
and the grounds of self-confidence of the Protector are of a well-established nature.
The analytical knowledges are characterized by the non-interruption of eloquence and so forth.

The bringing about of the welfare of the world is defined as great loving-kindness (mahāmaitrī). Great compassion (mahākṛpā) is the protection of those who suffer; joy (muditā) indeed has the characteristic of gladness; and equanimity (upekṣā) should be known as having the characteristic of being unmixed.

The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of a Buddha are held to be those which are considered [to be such]; since the Teacher cannot be overcome by them, they therefore possess the characteristic of being unassailable.
The knowledge of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā-jñāna*) is held to have the characteristic of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Anything else is not accepted as direct perception because it is partial.

(6.214) Whatever is the characteristic of conditioned phenomena and whatever is the characteristic of the unconditioned—their emptiness by means of that very [characteristic] is the emptiness of specific characteristics. (6.215)
This present [moment], being non-abiding, does not exist as past or future;
where these two are not perceived, that is called "non-apprehension.
That which is the state of that non-apprehension, being devoid of its own intrinsic nature—
The emptiness called "non-apprehension" consists in the absence of both permanence and destruction. (6.217) There is no composite form of entities because they arise from conditions;
the emptiness of that very composition is the "emptiness of non-existence. (6.218)
In brief, the five aggregates are designated by the term "existence" (bhāva).
The emptiness of those very aggregates is what is called the "emptiness of existence" (bhāva-śūnyatā). Non-existence (abhāva) is taught in brief as the unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Emptiness by way of that non-existence is the emptiness of the non-existence of that very thing.
The absence of intrinsic nature in primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is, however, the emptiness called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
"Nature is not something produced"; thus it is called "intrinsic nature.
For whether Buddhas arise or do not arise, emptiness is proclaimed as the ultimate reality of all things. (6.221–222)
"The limit of reality, suchness, and that which is emptiness of other-nature—
these are proclaimed in the system of the Perfection of Wisdom.
Thus [ends] the clear illumination of the rays of intelligence.
Just as one realizes an amalaka fruit held in the palm of one's own hand,
so too this entire triple world, unborn from the beginning, comes to cessation through the power of conventional truth. 6.224
He always generates compassion for the world that is without a protector, and his intention is ever set upon cessation; thereafter,
by means of his wisdom, he triumphs over all.
Through the power of the Sugata’s word,
he proceeds toward the further shore of the ocean of the Victor’s qualities; honored by these swans of living beings, he goes to that supreme state.
By the power of the auspicious wind, the royal swan, whose wings are formed from the reality of the vast white covering, [soars].
